title: Moral Panic at the Academy
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman responds to an AARE blog post opposing the review of Australian Professional Standards for Teachers by making the opposite case: the standards are ideologically driven, evidence-poor, and actively harmful because they mandate differentiation while ignoring explicit teaching, cognitive load theory, retrieval practice, and other evidence-based approaches. He identifies a structural irony—the standards protect evidence-blind practices while potentially marking evidence-informed whole-class teaching as non-compliant. The AARE academics' defense of teacher autonomy against 'pre-determined scripts' is framed by Ashman as a moral panic that conflates teacher freedom with the absence of standards, and he encourages readers to contribute to the review with evidence-informed critiques.
points: Australia's Professional Standards for Teachers omit explicit teaching, cognitive load theory, the worked example effect, retrieval practice, and spaced practice—all evidence-supported approaches.
Differentiation is required by the Standards despite limited research support, creating a perverse outcome where whole-class explicit teaching can be flagged as non-compliant.
The AARE academics defending the status quo frame teacher autonomy against 'pre-determined scripts,' but Ashman argues this conflates freedom with the absence of evidence-based accountability.

Ashman calls the resistance to standards reform a 'moral panic' because it mobilizes emotional appeals—nostalgia for beloved teachers—rather than evidence about what actually produces student learning.
The post serves as both critique and call to action, inviting readers to submit to the standards review with evidence-informed perspectives.
quotes: The Standards are poor. They are not based on evidence from cognitive science or high-quality education research. For example, they do not mention explicit teaching, cognitive load theory, the worked example effect, retrieval practice, spaced practice, or methods of checking for understanding.

There is little research evidence to support differentiation and yet it sits in the Standards while evidence-informed approaches do not. This shows the Standards are based more on ideology and romantic ideas of how the author/s would like the world to be than being based on how the world actually is.

The pernicious effect of having differentiation in the Standards is that a teacher using whole-class, explicit teaching may be seen by some as failing to differentiate. And so the evidence-blind practice defeats the evidence-informed one.

'Were they the ones that followed a pre-determined script and rigid lesson plan. Or was it an educator responsive to the young people in their care? Who adapted their approach by using a range of techniques to engage everyone in the room.'
I expect that many lecturers make some pretty disparaging remarks about this content, given it conflicts so deeply with their ideologies of teaching and education.
